newsitem.title: UK: Nepalese boy's future in hands of UK politicians.
newsitem.headline: Nepalese boy's future in hands of UK politicians.

text.p: The guardian of a young Nepalese man threatened with deportation staked his family's future in Britain on Tuesday by making an unusual appeal to two leading opposition politicians to adjudicate in the case.

Richard Morley, a computer software millionaire who brought Jay Khadka to Britain from Nepal in 1990, told a news conference he had decided to bring the matter to "a speedy conclusion" by placing it firmly in the political arena.
A High Court judge ruled that Home Secretary (interior minister) Michael Howard had been right to order the deportation of Kadkha, 20, although he agreed the decision might seem harsh.

Morley said he and his family would leave Britain without further ado if either Jack Straw or Alex Carlile, the home affairs spokesmen of the opposition Labour and Liberal Democrat parties, agreed with the deportation order.

"I believe their views are essential in the name of democracy and we will abide by what they decide," Morley, who has sent the papers of the case to Straw and Carlile as well as writing to Conservative Prime Minister John Major.
He said he had received around 1,000 letters of support from members of the British public. Khadka thanked the British people for their hospitality and support.
"I can't believe the deportation serves the British people and it is bad for the British image abroad," Morley said.
Their parliamentary campaign is being backed by Emma Nicholson, a Liberal Democrat member of parliament, who called Howard's decision "perverse, pernicious and political".
She said it was unfair and unkind to deport a boy who had been educated in Britain, had made his life here and did not constitute a burden on the state.
Morley brought Kadkha to Britain to honour a pact he made with the boy's father.
Basu Kadkha, a policeman in a remote area of Nepal, saved Morley's life when the millionaire collapsed with a punctured lung while on a mountaineering expedition in Nepal in 1988.
The policeman ran 60 miles (100 km) to the nearest telephone to summon help, but refused financial reward, instead imploring Morley to take care of his son if anything should happen to him.
Morley returned to Nepal to find that the elder Kadkha had died. He brought Jay back to Britain and made him his sole heir.
